lessons.title: Tags Carry Meaning
lessons.hook: A missing alt attribute turns a real photo into silence for a screen reader.

blocks.heading: The Tree Under the Page
blocks.body: Every tag becomes a node in two trees: the one the browser paints, and the accessibility tree that screen readers read instead of pixels. A plain `div` says nothing about what it holds; a `button` or `nav` announces its own job by name. Images carry no words at all unless you give them one: the `alt` attribute is the sentence a screen reader speaks in place of the picture. Skip it on a photo that matters and it becomes empty space. A purely decorative image gets `alt=""` so it is skipped on purpose, not by accident. Reading a tag's own attributes back in script is a quick way to check what actually shipped, not what you meant to write.

steps.say: Empty alt is a deliberate signal: skip this image, it carries no extra meaning.
A real alt survives even if the image never loads, so the data is not lost.
Grabbing both elements first keeps the comparison honest instead of guessing.
Printing `.alt.length` proves what actually reached the accessibility tree.

blocks.caption: Two images, two different reasons for their alt text.

blocks.prompt: say(id) is true only when the alt is a real description. The star is decorative, the thumbnail's alt was copied from the file name, and the map has a written sentence. What does this print?
blocks.hint: Run say in your head on each image: does it have words, and are those words anything more than the file name?
blocks.explain: thumb has words, but they are the file name, so the second test fails it. star is empty on purpose, so the first test fails it. Only map carries a sentence a screen reader can actually use.

blocks.prompt:
This page has one image, `#hero`, whose `alt` is still empty even though the photo is not decorative -- it is the page's main team photo.

Write a script that sets `#hero`'s `alt` to a real description of the photo, a few actual words, not the filename.

Example: alt could read something like "Three teammates high-fiving at a launch party".

tests.input: const alt = document.getElementById('hero').alt; return (alt && alt.trim().length > 5) ? 'ok' : 'alt is still empty or too short'
tests.name: alt is filled in

tests.input: const alt = document.getElementById('hero').alt.toLowerCase(); return alt.includes('team.jpg') ? 'alt still looks like a filename' : 'ok'
tests.name: not just the filename

blocks.hint: Set the element's alt property to a plain-language description, not the filename.
blocks.explain: Assigning alt describes the photo for anyone who cannot see it; an empty string said "nothing here," which was false since this image matters.

bullets: Tag names build the tree screen readers actually read.
Empty alt means decorative on purpose, not by accident.
A missing or filename-only alt turns real content into silence.
blocks.remember: If a screen reader cannot say it, the page has not really said it either.

blocks.say: Time to hunt real markup where alt text is missing, wrong, or just a filename.

lessons.exitLine: Time to hunt real markup where alt text is missing, wrong, or just a filename.
